section: One: what does a query cost?

One: what does a query cost?
\text{cost} = \frac{\text{tokens}_{\text{in}} \times p_{\text{in}} + \text{tokens}_{\text{out}} \times p_{\text{out}}}{1{,}000{,}000}







Bet before we compute


In a document pipeline — retrieval, long context, a short answer — which of the two terms dominates?





Input, and not by a little. You send thousands of tokens of retrieved passages to get back two hundred. Everyone optimises the answer length; the bill is on the question.

title: From a prototype to something a firm would run
section: Two things that change the arithmetic
text:
Two things that change the arithmetic


Cached input The reusable prefix — system prompt plus fixed context — billed at a discount when the provider serves it from cache.
Restructure the prompt so the fixed part comes first.

Routing Easy queries to a small model, hard ones to a frontier model.
Cost becomes a weighted average. Whether quality survives is a question for your evals, not for a vendor.

Two: is it worth it?
\text{break-even value per query} = \text{cost per query}
Below that line the system loses money on every call, and volume makes it worse rather than better.

Cost per query is arithmetic and you will get it right. Value per query is judgement, it is the number nobody can hand you, and it is the one the Board will ask about first.

Cost one query, then a thousand a day, then ten thousand.
Build the sensitivity table: across volume, across tiers, with and without caching.
Plot the chart: your eval score against your measured cost, one dot per model you tried. Drop everything that is dominated.
State your break-even value per query, and say whether you believe it.








The honest form of an estimate


One number is a guess with a decimal point. A sensitivity table is an estimate, because it shows what would have to be true for it to be wrong.

There is no buyer on the other side
A pool holds 100 ETH and 6,000,000 USDC. You want to buy ETH. Nobody is selling — there is no counterparty, no bid, no ask.

What determines the price you pay?





One rule, and only one:
x \cdot y = k
Take ETH out, the pool has less; put USDC in, it has more. The product must not change, and that alone fixes the price.

99.5%. It has learned the base rate and nothing else. Accuracy on rare events measures how rare the event is.

Three numbers that do mean something

They trade off. Catch more fraud and you block more good customers. There is no setting that is good at everything, and pretending otherwise is how these projects fail.

\text{cost} = (\text{blocked good} \times \text{cost of contact}) + (\text{missed fraud} \times \text{amount})
Put your numbers in. Sweep the threshold. The minimum is your answer, and it moves when the business changes.

Nobody in the room can tell you the right threshold. The cost table can, and building that table is the actual work.

GDPR Article 22: no solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effect, without safeguards — including meaningful human review.
Adverse action: the applicant is entitled to know what drove it.

So “the model said 0.31” is not a deployable answer. You need the largest contributions to that particular decision, in words a person can act on.

text:
Two definitions of fair, and you cannot have both


Equal approval rates The same share approved in each group.

Equal calibration A score of 0.7 means the same thing in each group.


When the base rates genuinely differ, these are mathematically incompatible. Not a bug, not a modelling failure — a theorem.
Which means someone has to choose, and write down why. That someone is a person, not a model.

The model has never read your contract, your filing, or last month’s board pack. It was trained before they existed, and it cannot open a file.

√252 applied to crypto Markets trade 252 days a year. Bitcoin trades 365. The formula is right, the constant is wrong, and the output looks perfectly reasonable.

Returns added up Cumulative return is not the sum of daily returns. Compounding is a product. Close enough to look right, wrong enough to matter.

Print head() and read it. Not glance — read. Is that number plausible as a daily return?
Plot before you model. A wrong unit is usually visible as a wrong axis.
Compute one number a second way. Cumulative return from first and last price, against the same thing from the return series. If they disagree, stop.

The assistant is fluent about code and blind about meaning. Units, calendars and conventions are exactly where it fails silently.

You will not learn these from this page. You will learn each one the first time it costs you a wrong number. This page is for when you forget which week that was.
The Wk column says where the term is introduced properly.

title: Glossary
section: Language models
text:
Language models








Term
In one line
Wk




LLM (large language model)
A model trained to predict the next piece of text, given all the text before it. Everything else it does is built on that one operation.
1


Token
The unit a model reads and writes: a chunk of characters, often part of a word. You are billed, limited and measured in tokens, not words.
1


Tokenizer
The component that cuts text into tokens. It is trained on a corpus, so text unlike that corpus (other languages, numbers, new names) cuts into more pieces.
1


Context window
Everything the model can see in one call: instructions, history, documents, and its own answer so far. Nothing outside it exists for the model.
1


Attention
How the model reads its context: to process each token it weighs every other token in the window, and decides how much each one matters. Every-token-with-every-token is why long contexts cost more than they look.
1


Weights
The numbers learned in training. They are frozen when you call the model; nothing you type changes them.
1


Prompt
The text you send. In production it is code: versioned, tested, and stored next to what it produced.
1–4


Temperature
How strictly the model follows its own probabilities when choosing the next token. T = 0 for extraction and anything auditable; higher for ideas.
2


Hallucination
A fluent output that is not supported by anything in the context — the model producing the shape of an answer where the facts are missing.
2


Embedding
A list of numbers representing a piece of text, arranged so that similar meanings are close together. Turns “similar” into a distance.
4


RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
Find the relevant passages in your documents first, put them in the context, then ask the model to answer from them — and cite them.
4


Structured output
Forcing the answer into a fixed shape (e.g. JSON with named fields). Guarantees the type, not the truth.
4


Fine-tuning
Further training of a model on your examples. Changes style and format well; is a poor way to add facts you will need to update or cite.
1, 4


Tool call
The model emits a structured request (“call get_price('BTC')”); your code runs it and returns the result into the context.
5


Agent
A model calling tools in a loop until it decides it is done. Every agent failure is a failure of that loop.
5


Prompt injection
Instructions hidden inside a document or web page that the model reads and then obeys.
5, 9


Eval (evaluation)
A fixed set of questions with known answers, run on every change, so “it seems better” becomes a number.
5


LLM-as-judge
Using one model to grade another’s answers. Useful and cheap; biased, so it is itself checked against human grades.
5


Software 1.0 / 2.0 / 3.0
The same decision written as a rule, as a model fitted to data, or as an instruction in plain language. Knowing which one a problem needs is most of the job.
1, 3

title: Glossary
section: Data and analysis
text:
Data and analysis








Term
In one line
Wk




Notebook
A document mixing code, its output and prose, run cell by cell. Ours run in Google Colab.
1


DataFrame
A table in Python (pandas), with named columns and an index — usually dates, for us.
2


Return (simple)
Percentage change from one price to the next: P_t / P_{t-1} − 1.
2


Log return
ln(P_t / P_{t-1}). Unlike simple returns, log returns add up over time.
2


Cumulative return
Total growth over a period. With simple returns it is a product of (1 + r), not a sum.
2


Volatility (annualised)
Standard deviation of daily returns, scaled to a year by √(trading days): 252 for stock markets, 365 for crypto.
2


Drawdown
The fall from the highest value reached so far. Maximum drawdown is the worst such fall in the period.
2


Join
Putting two tables side by side on a shared key (for us, the date). The choice of which rows survive is a modelling decision.
2


Forward-fill (ffill)
Filling a missing value with the last known one. It invents data — sometimes that is the right choice, always it must be said.
2


Units
What a number measures: percent or decimal, dollars or thousands. Not in the data; always your responsibility.
2


Snapshot
A dated copy of the data behind a result, so the number can be reproduced when the source changes.
2


Reproducibility
Someone else, on another machine, gets your number. If it needs you in the room, it is not a result yet.
2

title: Glossary
section: Machine learning and evaluation
text:
Machine learning and evaluation








Term
In one line
Wk




Feature
What you know at time t, used as input.
3


Target
What happens after t — the thing you are trying to predict.
3


Horizon
How far after t the target is measured.
3


Base rate
How often the outcome happens anyway. Predicting “always the most common outcome” scores the base rate with no model at all.
3


Baseline
The simplest reasonable alternative your model must beat — the base rate, a rule, last week’s value.
3


Train / test split
Fit on one part of the data, measure on another the model never saw.
3


Leakage
Information from the future (or from the test set) getting into what the model learns from. Produces results that look excellent and are worthless.
3


Walk-forward
Repeatedly fit on the past and test on the next period, moving forward in time. The honest split for anything with a date on it.
3, 7


Accuracy
Share of predictions that were right. Meaningless without the base rate.
3


Precision / recall
Of what you flagged, how much was right / of what was there, how much you flagged. You trade one for the other with the threshold.
3


AUC
How well a model ranks positives above negatives, across all thresholds. 0.5 is a coin.
3


Threshold
The probability above which you act. Set it from the costs of the two kinds of error, not at 0.5 by habit.
3


Calibration
Whether “70% likely” happens about 70% of the time. A model can rank well and be badly calibrated.
3


SHAP
A method that splits a single prediction into contributions from each feature. Explains the model, not the world.
9

title: Glossary
section: Markets and backtesting
text:
Markets and backtesting








Term
In one line
Wk




Backtest
Running a trading rule on historical data as if you had traded it. The easiest result in finance to fool yourself with.
7


Transaction costs
Fees, spread and price impact paid on every trade. Many strategies that work on paper do not survive them.
7


Survivorship bias
Testing only on assets that still exist today, which quietly removes the ones that failed.
7


Multiple testing
Try enough strategies and one will look good by chance. The more you tried, the less the best one means.
7


Regime change
The market’s behaviour shifts (rates, volatility, regulation), and a pattern that held stops holding.
7


Sharpe ratio
Average excess return divided by its volatility — return per unit of risk.
7


Model risk
The risk of loss from a model that is wrong, or used where it was not meant to be. Banks are required to manage it.
7

title: Glossary
section: Crypto and DeFi
text:
Crypto and DeFi








Term
In one line
Wk




Blockchain
A shared ledger that many independent computers keep in agreement, where past entries are very hard to change.
8


On-chain data
Everything recorded on the ledger — transfers, balances, contract calls — public, and readable by anyone.
2, 8


Wallet / address
An address holds assets; a wallet holds the private key that can move them. Whoever has the key has the assets.
8


Smart contract
A program deployed on a blockchain that runs exactly as written when called. Including its bugs.
8


Gas
The fee paid to the network to execute a transaction or a contract call.
8


Stablecoin
A token designed to hold a fixed value, usually one US dollar (USDC, USDT). Only as stable as what backs it.
8


DeFi (decentralised finance)
Financial services — trading, lending, borrowing — run by smart contracts instead of intermediaries.
8


DEX (decentralised exchange)
An exchange run by a smart contract. Most use a liquidity pool instead of an order book.
8


Liquidity pool
Two tokens deposited in a contract that anyone can trade against.
8


AMM (automated market maker)
The rule that prices a pool. The classic one: x · y = k — the product of the two balances stays constant, so every trade moves the price.
1, 8


Slippage / price impact
The difference between the quoted price and what you actually pay, because your own trade moves the price.
1, 8


LP (liquidity provider)
Someone who deposits tokens into a pool and earns a share of trading fees.
8


Impermanent loss
What an LP gives up, compared with simply holding the two tokens, when their relative price moves. “Impermanent” only if the price comes back.
8


TVL (total value locked)
The value of assets deposited in a protocol. A size measure, not a profit measure — and easy to inflate.
8


Lending protocol
A contract that lends deposited assets to borrowers who post more collateral than they borrow.
8


Collateral ratio / liquidation
How much collateral backs a loan. Fall below the threshold and the protocol sells your collateral automatically.
8


Staking
Locking tokens to help secure a network (or a protocol) in exchange for a yield.
8


Oracle
A service that brings off-chain data (e.g. a price) onto the chain. A wrong or manipulated oracle price is a classic DeFi failure.
8

title: Glossary
section: Regulation and responsible use
text:
Regulation and responsible use








Term
In one line
Wk




EU AI Act
EU regulation that classifies AI uses by risk — prohibited, high-risk, limited, minimal — with obligations rising accordingly. Credit scoring is high-risk.
4


MiCA
EU Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation: licensing and rules for crypto-asset service providers and stablecoin issuers.
8


ESMA
The EU securities markets authority; issues guidance under MiCA and on AI in investment services.
8


GDPR
EU data protection law. For us: personal data does not go into an AI tool without a legal basis — in this course, not at all.
2, 9


Human oversight
A named person who can understand, question and override the system’s output — and actually does.
9


Red-teaming
Attacking your own system on purpose to find how it fails before someone else does.
9

title: Syllabus
text: This is the web version of the course design document. The original is available as Word document; it still shows the Monday slot proposed in September. The timetable agreed with ESE is Wednesdays 10:00–13:00 from 23 September, and the dates on this page and on the schedule are the agreed ones. Readings may be updated before and during the course; the student is informed in writing.

title: Syllabus
section: Course description
text:
Course description
This applied short course teaches how artificial intelligence is actually built into business and fintech workflows in 2026: not by describing tools, but by using them. Working one-to-one with the tutor, the student writes Python in Google Colab with an AI coding assistant, learns to read and verify what the assistant produces, and progressively builds a portfolio of working artefacts: a reproducible data-analysis pipeline on market and on-chain data, a supervised model with an honest evaluation, an LLM application with retrieval and tool use, a backtest that avoids the classic mistakes, and a DeFi protocol analysis. The final capstone assembles these into an AI-enabled product prototype with an implementation roadmap.
Finance and digital assets — equities, cryptocurrencies, DeFi — are the running thread from week 2, so that every technique is practised on data the student cares about. Product and project management, the student’s professional background, is used as the lens for framing, evaluating and presenting what has been built, rather than as a separate topic. Ethics, regulation (EU AI Act, MiCA), model risk and human oversight are taught in context, at the point in the course where each becomes concrete.
The course deliberately pushes beyond a “managerial overview”: the student leaves able to prototype, test and critically evaluate AI systems, and therefore to manage AI projects and products with technical credibility.

title: Syllabus
section: Prerequisites
text:
Prerequisites
No prior programming experience is required, but the student must be willing to write and run code from the first session. A degree-level background in economics or business, familiarity with spreadsheets and KPIs, and English at C1 are assumed. The student needs a laptop, a Google account (for Colab) and a GitHub account. Nothing needs to be installed locally.

title: Syllabus
section: Aims
text:
Aims

Give a working (not mathematical) understanding of how modern AI systems — machine learning models and large language models — behave, fail and are evaluated.
Make the student productive in Python with AI coding assistants, able to reproduce, verify and extend analyses rather than trust outputs blindly.
Teach the full loop of a data-driven decision: question, data, model, honest evaluation, decision rule, KPI.
Build LLM applications end-to-end: API calls, structured output, retrieval-augmented generation, tool-using agents, and evaluation suites.
Apply these skills to financial markets, digital assets and DeFi with disciplined evaluation (leakage, overfitting, costs, regime change, protocol risk).
Embed responsible-AI practice — privacy, security, bias, explainability, EU AI Act and MiCA, model governance and human oversight — into every artefact.
Produce and defend an AI-enabled product prototype with a credible implementation roadmap.

title: Syllabus
section: Learning outcomes
text:
Learning outcomes
On successful completion the student will be able to:

Explain how LLMs and supervised models work at an operational level and distinguish suitable from unsuitable business applications.
Use Python in Colab with an AI assistant to acquire, clean, join and visualise business, market and on-chain data reproducibly.
Train and evaluate a supervised model against a baseline using appropriate (time-aware) validation and metrics, and translate predictions into decisions and KPIs.
Build an LLM application with structured output, retrieval over documents and tool use, and measure its quality with an evaluation set.
Design and run a backtest that explicitly controls for look-ahead bias, overfitting, transaction costs and regime change, and critique trading-model claims.
Analyse a digital-asset or DeFi use case through business-model, data and risk lenses using real protocol data.
Assess ethical, privacy, security, regulatory and governance implications of an AI system and design proportionate controls and human oversight.
Frame, build, test and present an AI-enabled product prototype and defend its implementation roadmap.

title: Syllabus
section: Teaching method and weekly rhythm
text:
Teaching method and weekly rhythm
Every Wednesday session follows the same shape: 20 minutes reviewing the previous homework together (the student walks the tutor through the notebook), roughly 50 minutes of concepts, about 90 minutes of lab work in Colab with the tutor at the student’s side, and 20 minutes to brief the next homework. The tutor demonstrates, then the student does the same thing on different data. The AI assistant is used openly and constantly; the skill being taught is how to direct it, read its output and catch its errors.
Homework is set every week, requires 4–6 hours, and is due on Tuesday at 23:59 so it can open the following session. Each piece of homework is a folder in the student’s course repository; the artefacts accumulate into the capstone rather than being discarded. Homework is formative (reviewed and discussed, not marked) but completion of all weekly work is a condition for certification.

title: Syllabus
section: Session plan
text:
Session plan

Session 1 — Wed 23 Sep — How LLMs work, and how we will work







0:00–0:20
Orientation: course contract, tools, repository, weekly rhythm, assessment.




0:20–1:10
LLMs at a working level: tokens, context window, sampling, why models hallucinate, embeddings, tool use, agents. What changed between 2023 and 2026 and what it means for business use.


1:10–2:40
Lab: Colab and GitHub set-up; first notebook — download daily prices for BTC, an equity and an index (yfinance/CoinGecko), compute returns, plot. The core loop: ask the assistant → run → read the error → ask again → verify against a known fact.


2:40–3:00
Prompting that matters at work: system vs user instructions, examples, asking for structure, forcing sources. Homework brief.



Homework: HW1 — Notebook with three assets (one equity, one cryptocurrency, one index): daily returns, summary statistics, one chart that answers a question. Plus a 200-word note describing one thing the assistant got wrong and how you caught it.


Session 2 — Wed 30 Sep — Data analysis with AI as pair programmer







0:00–0:20
HW1 review.




0:20–1:10
pandas by doing: tidy data, joins, resampling, missing values, look-ups. Descriptive vs predictive questions. Charts that answer a question. Data provenance, seeds and pinned versions (reproducibility); what must never be pasted into an AI tool (privacy).


1:10–2:40
Lab: join market data with an external series (FRED rates, Google Trends, on-chain active addresses). Sanity checks: units, date alignment, known events visible in the chart. Let the assistant write the code, then break it and fix it.


2:40–3:00
Homework brief.



Homework: HW2 — Exploratory analysis memo: one question (“does X co-move with Y?”, “what happened to Z around event E?”), a reproducible notebook, a one-page memo with the decisive chart, and an AI-use disclosure.


Session 3 — Wed 7 Oct — Machine learning through one problem; from prediction to decision







0:00–0:20
HW2 review.




0:20–1:10
Supervised learning: features, target, train/test, why time series need time-aware splits, overfitting, baselines, metrics (accuracy vs precision/recall, MAE), base rates and calibration.


1:10–2:40
Lab: predict next-week direction or volatility regime with logistic regression and gradient boosting; compare with a naive baseline; introduce leakage on purpose (random split, future features) and watch the score lie. Walk-forward validation.


2:40–3:00
From prediction to decision: expected value, thresholds, KPI design, when a human must decide. Homework brief.



Homework: HW3 — Model vs baseline with honest, time-aware evaluation, and a section titled “What would have to be true for this to be useful” (decision rule, KPI, cost of errors).


Session 4 — Wed 14 Oct — LLM applications I — API, structured output, retrieval (RAG)







0:00–0:20
HW3 review.




0:20–1:00
Calling an LLM from Python: messages, temperature, JSON/structured output, cost and latency. Embeddings and similarity. The RAG pipeline: chunk → embed → retrieve → generate with citations; where it fails.


1:00–2:30
Lab: build a RAG system over a small finance corpus — risk sections of three 10-K filings, the Bitcoin and Uniswap whitepapers, a MiCA summary. Ask questions, inspect retrieved chunks, catch wrong answers.


2:30–3:00
EU AI Act in 30 minutes: risk tiers, general-purpose model obligations, transparency duties; what applies to a fintech assistant. Homework brief.



Homework: HW4 — Extend the RAG system with a corpus of your choice; write 10 test questions with expected answers; record hits and misses and explain the misses.


Session 5 — Wed 21 Oct — LLM applications II — agents, tool use, evaluation; the product lens







0:00–0:20
HW4 review.




0:20–1:00
Agents = LLM + tools + loop. Function calling. When an agent beats a fixed pipeline and when it does not. Failure modes, cost control, prompt injection. Evaluation: golden sets, LLM-as-judge, regression tests.


1:00–2:20
Lab: give the model tools (get_price, get_news, run_analysis) and build a “research analyst” agent that answers “summarise the last 30 days of asset X with numbers”; write an evaluation set and score it.


2:20–3:00
The product lens (the student’s expertise applied): AI product brief — users, value, data, guardrails, metrics, unit economics of inference. Minor Applied Case Brief specification.



Homework: Reading Week assignment — Minor Applied Case Brief (40%): 1,500 words plus an 8-minute presentation treating the system built in weeks 4–5 as a product: problem, users, evidence from evaluations, risks, controls, success metrics. Due Sunday 1 November.


Reading Week — 26 Oct – 1 Nov — no class








Independent work on the Minor Applied Case Brief. One optional 45-minute online office hour.







Session 6 — Wed 4 Nov — Minor presentation; fintech landscape; capstone scoping







0:00–0:45
Minor Applied Case presentation, questions, written feedback.




0:45–2:00
Where AI actually earns money in fintech: payments, credit scoring, fraud and AML, KYC, robo-advice, customer operations. Build/buy/partner. What regulators expect: model risk management, explainability in credit decisions, financial inclusion.


2:00–3:00
Capstone scoping workshop: three candidate topics, pick one, define deliverables and a weekly plan.



Homework: HW6 — Capstone proposal (one page): question, data sources, method, deliverable, risks, week-by-week plan.


Session 7 — Wed 11 Nov — AI in markets and trading — backtesting done honestly







0:00–0:20
HW6 review and proposal sign-off.




0:20–1:10
Market data and features; signals; backtesting logic. The pitfalls: look-ahead bias, survivorship, overfitting and multiple testing, transaction costs and slippage, regime change. Why most published crypto ML results are wrong. LLM-derived sentiment signals and how to test them.


1:10–2:40
Lab: vectorised momentum backtest with costs; add leakage deliberately and watch the Sharpe ratio jump; walk-forward validation; add an LLM-derived news feature and test it honestly.


2:40–3:00
Model risk in 20 minutes: model inventory, validation, monitoring, kill-switches. Homework brief.



Homework: HW7 — Backtest of one strategy with costs and walk-forward validation, a completed pitfall checklist, and one LLM-derived feature tested against the baseline. No live trading; educational simulation only.


Session 8 — Wed 18 Nov — Digital assets, on-chain data and DeFi







0:00–0:20
HW7 review.




0:20–1:10
Blockchain fundamentals at business level; wallets, exchanges, stablecoins; smart contracts; automated market makers (x·y = k), impermanent loss, lending protocols, staking. Protocol risks: smart contract, oracle, governance, depeg, liquidity.


1:10–2:30
Lab: pull protocol data (DefiLlama TVL and fees, CoinGecko, Etherscan/Dune); simulate an AMM pool and liquidity-provider returns; analyse one protocol’s token economics; use the LLM to summarise its governance forum and check the summary against the source.


2:30–3:00
MiCA and ESMA in 30 minutes: what is regulated, who needs a licence, what it means for a product. Homework brief.



Homework: HW8 — Protocol analysis through business-model, data and risk lenses, with at least one quantitative element (LP simulation, TVL/fee analysis or token-flow analysis).


Session 9 — Wed 25 Nov — Responsible AI applied to the capstone; red-team







0:00–0:20
HW8 review.




0:20–1:10
Bias and fairness, explainability (SHAP on the week-3 model), privacy, security of LLM applications (prompt injection, data exfiltration), dependence on third-party models, designing human oversight. The AI risk and controls canvas.


1:10–2:40
Lab: red-team the student’s capstone pipeline — adversarial inputs, corrupted data, leakage audit, prompt injection; fill the risk and controls canvas; formative feedback on the prototype.


2:40–3:00
Homework brief.



Homework: HW9 — Near-final capstone prototype with a completed risk and controls canvas and a log of what the red-team found and how it was fixed.


Session 10 — Wed 2 Dec — Implementation, operating model and capstone studio







0:00–0:20
HW9 review.




0:20–1:10
From prototype to production: build/buy/partner, data and technology readiness, roles and governance, cost of inference at scale, change adoption, measuring value, pilot-to-production roadmap.


1:10–2:40
Studio: finalise the prototype and roadmap; rehearse the final presentation.


2:40–3:00
Course wrap-up and reflection.



Homework: Final AI Strategy and Prototype Portfolio (60%) due Sunday 6 December. Final oral presentation in Revision Week (proposed Wednesday 9 December, 10:00; 8 December is a holiday).

title: Syllabus
section: Assessment
text:
Assessment









Assessment
Weight
Specification
Timing




Minor Applied Case Brief
40%
Individual 1,500-word brief plus 8-minute presentation. The LLM application built in weeks 4–5 is treated as a product: problem, users, evidence from evaluation, risks, controls, success metrics. The working notebook is submitted with the brief.
Brief due Sun 1 Nov (Reading Week). Presentation Wed 4 Nov.


Final AI Strategy and Prototype Portfolio
60%
Individual capstone: decision memo (2,000 words), a working prototype or reproducible workflow in the course repository, evidence of testing and evaluation, risk and controls canvas, implementation roadmap. Topic in fintech, market analytics, digital assets/DeFi or another approved business context.
Portfolio due Sun 6 Dec. Oral presentation in Revision Week (7–13 Dec).




Marking criteria

15% Problem framing and business relevance
25% Quality and critical use of data, evidence and AI methods
20% Technical artefact: does it work, is it reproducible, is it honestly evaluated
20% Risk, ethics, governance and human oversight
20% Clarity, professional communication and reflection

Weekly homework is formative and reviewed at the start of each session; completing all weekly work is a condition for the ESE certificate. No written examination is proposed for the Final Exams period (14–18 December).

title: Syllabus
section: Responsible use of AI and financial context
text:
Responsible use of AI and financial context
AI tools are not only permitted but expected. Every submission discloses which tools were used, for what, and how outputs were verified; the analysis and judgement must remain the student’s own. No confidential, personal or commercially sensitive data may be entered into AI services. All activities involving securities, cryptocurrencies or DeFi are educational simulations and analytical exercises; nothing in the course constitutes investment advice and the student is never required to trade or commit funds.

title: Syllabus
section: Materials and channels
text:
Materials and channels



Channel
Purpose




GitHub
Single source of truth. The course repository (NiccoloSalvini/ese-ai, mirrored on this site) holds one folder per week with the session notebook, the concept cards and the homework. The student’s private repository ese-ai-fintech holds week-NN/hw/ and capstone/. Homework is pushed by Tuesday 23:59.


Google Colab
Runtime for all code. API keys stored in Colab Secrets, never in notebooks. Free tier is sufficient for the whole course.


Moodle
Official mirror once available: syllabus, one section per week linking here, submission points and written feedback for the two formal assessments, grades.


Telegram (or WhatsApp)
Quick questions between sessions, office-hour scheduling, links. Not for deliverables.


LLM access
Google AI Studio API key (free tier) for all API work in Colab, with OpenAI-compatible code so it ports to other providers. The student’s own chat subscription (ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini) for day-to-day assistance. Optional: a small OpenAI/Anthropic API budget for comparison in weeks 4–5.


Data
yfinance, CoinGecko, FRED, DefiLlama, Etherscan and Dune (free tiers); SEC EDGAR for filings; protocol whitepapers and governance forums.



Weekly cycle: Wednesday lesson; notes and homework published on GitHub and Moodle by Thursday; homework due Tuesday 23:59; reviewed together at the start of the following Wednesday.

title: Syllabus
section: Core and recommended resources
text:
Core and recommended resources

Mollick, E. (2024). Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI. Portfolio. (Weeks 1–2.)
Lopez de Prado, M. (2018). Advances in Financial Machine Learning. Wiley — chapters on labelling, cross-validation and backtesting. (Weeks 3 and 7.)
Harvey, C. R., Liu, Y. and Zhu, H. (2016). “…and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns.” Review of Financial Studies. (Week 7.)
Narayanan, A. and Clark, J. (2017). “Bitcoin’s Academic Pedigree.” Communications of the ACM. (Week 8.)
Adams, H. et al. (2021). Uniswap v3 Core (whitepaper); Nakamoto, S. (2008). Bitcoin whitepaper. (Weeks 4 and 8.)
European Commission — EU AI Act resources; ESMA — MiCA and crypto-asset resources; NIST AI Risk Management Framework and Generative AI Profile. (Weeks 4, 8, 9.)
BIS — publications on AI in finance and DeFi. (Weeks 6 and 8.)
Provider documentation: Google AI Studio / Gemini API, OpenAI API, Anthropic API; scikit-learn and pandas user guides. (Throughout.)

Readings may be updated before and during the course to reflect developments in tools and regulation; the student will be informed in writing.

title: Syllabus
section: Academic policies
text:
Academic policies
ESE attendance, academic integrity, late-submission, mitigating-circumstances and other academic policies apply. Reasonable changes may be made to content, tools, readings or activities; the student will be informed of material changes in writing.

title: Week 10 — Implementation and operating model; capstone studio
text:
ESE · AI for Business and FinTech · Wednesday 2 December 2026
Lighter notebook than usual: it is a set of calculators and templates you will reuse in your portfolio, plus one final checks cell that inspects your repo before you submit. Everything runs offline — no API key, no network. Replace every # <-- your number with the figures from your capstone; the defaults are illustrative.
Cells marked 🔍 CHECK contain something you must verify before moving on.
# Nothing new to install this week; pandas/numpy/matplotlib ship with Colab.
# (Kept so the notebook has the same shape as the others: Runtime ▸ Run all must work from a clean runtime.)
import warnings, numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
pd.set_option("display.width", 140); pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda x: f"{x:,.4f}")
print("pandas", pd.__version__, "| numpy", np.__version__)

title: Week 10 — Implementation and operating model; capstone studio
section: Block B — From prototype to production, as decisions with numbers
text:
Block B — From prototype to production, as decisions with numbers

B1. Build / buy / partner — the week-6 table, now for your capstone
Same scoring table as in week 6 (criteria × weight × option score), but the row labels are now the components of your pipeline. Score 1–5 per cell. The weights are yours to defend; the arithmetic is not.

criteria = pd.DataFrame({
    "weight": [0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.10],
}, index=["time to a working pilot", "control over data and prompts", "cost at target volume",
          "vendor / lock-in risk", "auditability (model risk, AI Act)", "skills you actually have"])
scores = pd.DataFrame({                         # 1 = bad, 5 = good      # <-- your numbers
    "build (own code + API model)": [4, 5, 4, 3, 4, 3],
    "buy (SaaS product)":           [5, 2, 2, 2, 3, 5],
    "partner (vendor builds on your data)": [3, 3, 3, 2, 3, 4],
}, index=criteria.index)

weighted = scores.mul(criteria["weight"], axis=0)
table = pd.concat([criteria, scores], axis=1)
table.loc["WEIGHTED TOTAL"] = [criteria["weight"].sum()] + list(weighted.sum())

🔍 CHECK. Change one weight by 0.10 (take it from another row so they still sum to 1). Does the ranking flip? If a decision flips on a 0.10 weight change, the table is not deciding — you are, and the memo should say so and give the real reason.


B2. Cost of inference at scale — the calculator
Price is per million tokens, and input and output are priced differently. The numbers below are illustrative tiers (check the provider’s page on the day you write the memo; they change every few months). Cached input is what providers charge when the same long prefix (system prompt + retrieved documents) is reused — typically a large discount.

# USD per 1M tokens — ILLUSTRATIVE tiers, not a quote. Replace with the provider page the day you decide.
PRICES = pd.DataFrame({
    "input":        [0.10, 1.00, 5.00],
    "cached_input": [0.025, 0.25, 1.25],   # ~75% discount on the cached part of the prompt
    "output":       [0.40, 4.00, 15.00],
}, index=["small", "mid", "frontier"])
PRICES



🔍 CHECK — the assistant’s cost estimate
You asked the assistant: “estimate the monthly cost of my RAG assistant: ~8,000-token prompt (system + 6 retrieved chunks + question), ~300-token answer, 20,000 queries a month on the frontier model.” It produced the cell below. It runs, it prints a plausible number. It is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude. Write your bet for the true monthly cost first, then find the error. Ten minutes; one hint after five.

# --- as produced by the assistant (do not trust) ---
tokens_out   = 300
queries_month = 20_000
tier = "frontier"

cost_per_query  = tokens_out / 1e6 * PRICES.loc[tier, "output"]
cost_per_month  = cost_per_query * queries_month
print(f"cost per query: ${cost_per_query:.4f}   |   monthly: ${cost_per_month:,.0f}")



Solution (open after you have tried)

The estimate prices only the output tokens. In a RAG system the prompt is mostly input: system instructions plus retrieved chunks plus the question — here 8,000 tokens against 300 of answer. Input is cheaper per token, but there is 27× more of it. The correct figure is
cost = tokens_in × price_in + tokens_out × price_out (all per 1M)
= 8,000/1e6 × 5.00 + 300/1e6 × 15.00 = 0.0400 + 0.0045 = $0.0445 per query, i.e. $890/month, against the assistant’s $90. Off by ~10×, and always in the same direction: the assistant’s mental model of “a query” is a chat turn, where input and output are similar in size. Yours is a document pipeline, where input dominates.
Rule for the memo: any cost figure must show tokens_in and tokens_out separately, with the two prices next to them. If you cannot see both, the number is not verified.


# Corrected: the calculator you will reuse. Input and output priced separately; caching applied to the cached share of input.
def cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, tier, cache_hit_rate=0.0, cached_share_of_input=0.0, prices=PRICES):
    """USD per query.
    cache_hit_rate       : share of queries whose cached prefix is actually served from cache (0..1)
    cached_share_of_input: share of the input tokens that belong to the reusable prefix (system prompt + fixed context)
    """
    p = prices.loc[tier]
    cached_tokens   = tokens_in * cached_share_of_input * cache_hit_rate
    uncached_tokens = tokens_in - cached_tokens
    return (uncached_tokens * p["input"] + cached_tokens * p["cached_input"] + tokens_out * p["output"]) / 1e6

tokens_in, tokens_out, queries_month = 8_000, 300, 20_000        # <-- your numbers (count them with tiktoken on your real prompt)
for tier in PRICES.index:
    cq = cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, tier)
    print(f"{tier:9s}: ${cq:.4f} per query  |  ${cq*queries_month:,.0f} per month  "
          f"(input share of cost: {tokens_in/1e6*PRICES.loc[tier,'input']/cq:.0%})")



B3. Sensitivity: volume × model tier, with and without caching
A sensitivity table is the honest form of a cost estimate: it shows the reader where the number breaks. Two tables — no caching, then with a realistic cache (say 60% of the prompt is a fixed prefix, served from cache 80% of the time).

volumes = [1_000, 5_000, 20_000, 100_000, 500_000]         # queries per month
def monthly_table(**kw):
    return pd.DataFrame({tier: [cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, tier, **kw) * v for v in volumes]
                         for tier in PRICES.index}, index=pd.Index(volumes, name="queries/month")).round(0)

print("Monthly cost (USD), no caching")
display(monthly_table())
print("\nMonthly cost (USD), 60% of prompt is a cacheable prefix, hit rate 80%")
display(monthly_table(cache_hit_rate=0.8, cached_share_of_input=0.6))



B4. Routing and the break-even value per query
Two decisions hide in every cost line. Routing: send the easy queries to the small model and only the hard ones to the frontier one — the cost is a weighted average, the quality is whatever your evals from week 5 say it is. Break-even: a query is worth running only if the value it creates exceeds its cost; below the break-even value per query, the system loses money on every call however good it is.
Before running: write your bet — at what monthly volume does the frontier model, with no routing, exceed a $2,000/month budget?

BUDGET_PER_MONTH = 2_000.0                                  # <-- your number
VALUE_PER_QUERY  = 0.05                                     # <-- your number: what one answered query is worth (time saved × hourly cost, or revenue)

grid = np.logspace(3, 6, 200)                              # 1k .. 1M queries/month
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

# left: monthly cost vs volume by tier + a routed mix
routed = lambda v: v * (0.8 * cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, "small") + 0.2 * cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, "frontier"))
for tier in PRICES.index:
    ax[0].plot(grid, [cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, tier) * v for v in grid], label=tier)
ax[0].plot(grid, [routed(v) for v in grid], "--", label="routed 80% small / 20% frontier")
ax[0].axhline(BUDGET_PER_MONTH, color="k", lw=0.8); ax[0].text(1_100, BUDGET_PER_MONTH * 1.15, "budget")
ax[0].set_xscale("log"); ax[0].set_yscale("log"); ax[0].set_xlabel("queries / month"); ax[0].set_ylabel("USD / month")
ax[0].set_title("Monthly cost by tier"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8)

# right: value minus cost per query by tier (break-even = where the bar crosses zero)
margin = pd.Series({t: VALUE_PER_QUERY - cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, t) for t in PRICES.index})
margin.plot.bar(ax=ax[1], color=["#4c9a2a" if m > 0 else "#c0392b" for m in margin])
ax[1].axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax[1].set_title(f"Value per query ({VALUE_PER_QUERY:.2f}) minus cost, by tier"); ax[1].set_ylabel("USD / query")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for tier in PRICES.index:
    be_volume = BUDGET_PER_MONTH / cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, tier)
    print(f"{tier:9s}: budget exhausted at {be_volume:>10,.0f} queries/month | break-even value per query = ${cost_per_query(tokens_in, tokens_out, tier):.4f}")
print(f"routed   : budget exhausted at {BUDGET_PER_MONTH / (routed(1)):>10,.0f} queries/month")

🔍 CHECK. Compare the frontier break-even volume with your bet. Then ask the question the chart cannot answer: is the frontier model actually better on your golden set from week 5? If the routed mix scores within your tolerance on the evals, the cost line is the decision. If you have no evals, you cannot route — you can only guess.


B5. Latency budget
Users notice latency before they notice quality. Sum the stages; compare with the target for your use case (a chat assistant tolerates ~5 s; a check inside a payment flow tolerates ~300 ms). Generation time is tokens_out / tokens_per_second, and it is usually the biggest line.

latency = pd.DataFrame({
    "ms": [40, 120, 350, 700, 300 / 60 * 1000, 30],       # <-- your numbers; generation = tokens_out / tokens_per_s * 1000
}, index=["network + auth", "embed the query", "vector search (top-6)", "time to first token (frontier)",
          "generate 300 tokens at 60 tok/s", "post-processing / guardrail"])
latency["cumulative_ms"] = latency["ms"].cumsum()
TARGET_MS = 5_000                                           # <-- your number
display(latency.round(0))
total = latency["ms"].sum()
print(f"total ≈ {total:,.0f} ms vs target {TARGET_MS:,} ms → {'OK' if total <= TARGET_MS else 'OVER BUDGET'}; "
      f"generation is {latency.loc['generate 300 tokens at 60 tok/s','ms']/total:.0%} of the total")

🔍 CHECK. Halve tokens_out (shorter answers, or a structured answer instead of prose). What happens to latency and to cost per query at the same time? This is the one lever that improves both — write it in the roadmap.

This cell inspects a repo folder and reports the mechanical part of the review checklist in notes.md. In Colab, mount Drive or clone your repo first, then set REPO_ROOT to the capstone/ folder. If the path does not exist it falls back to the current directory so the cell always runs. It does not judge content — that is the review pass with the tutor.

import os, re, json
from pathlib import Path

REPO_ROOT = Path("capstone")                                  # <-- your path, e.g. Path("/content/ese-ai-fintech/capstone")

for p in sorted(files)[:60]:
    print(f"  {p.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)}  ({p.stat().st_size/1024:,.0f} KB)")

def nb_stats(path):
    """(code cells, cells with error outputs, has 'Take-home' cell) for one notebook."""
    nb = json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    cells = nb.get("cells", [])
    n_code = sum(c["cell_type"] == "code" for c in cells)
    n_err = sum(any(o.get("output_type") == "error" for o in c.get("outputs", [])) for c in cells if c["cell_type"] == "code")
    take_home = any("take-home" in "".join(c.get("source", "")).lower() for c in cells)
    return n_code, n_err, take_home

notebooks = [p for p in files if p.suffix == ".ipynb"]

Today the working object is a protocol: a program that holds money and follows rules anyone can read. We simulate the most important one (a constant-product market maker) from its one equation, then read real protocol data through public APIs, then look at a protocol through a risk canvas and through MiCA.
Every number on the whiteboard today gets recomputed here. Cells marked 🔍 CHECK contain assistant-style code with a planted error: find it before opening the solution.
!pip -q install yfinance google-genai
# --- course helper: price loader with fallbacks (run this cell once per session) ---
import warnings, numpy as np, pandas as pd
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

def load_prices(tickers, start="2022-01-01", end=None, cache_dir="data"):
    """Daily close prices, one column per ticker.
    1) try yfinance (live)  2) try a CSV snapshot in data/  3) synthetic random walk (pipeline test only)."""
    import os
    os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
    key = "_".join(t.replace("^", "") for t in tickers)
    snap = os.path.join(cache_dir, f"prices_{key}.csv")
    try:
        import yfinance as yf
        raw = yf.download(tickers, start=start, end=end, auto_adjust=True, progress=False)
        px = raw["Close"] if isinstance(raw.columns, pd.MultiIndex) else raw[["Close"]].rename(columns={"Close": tickers[0]})
        px = px.dropna(how="all")
        if len(px) < 50:
            raise RuntimeError("empty download")
        px.to_csv(snap)
        print(f"[live] {px.shape[0]} rows from yfinance; snapshot saved to {snap}")
        return px
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[warn] yfinance failed ({type(e).__name__}); trying snapshot")
    if os.path.exists(snap):
        px = pd.read_csv(snap, index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
        print(f"[snapshot] {px.shape[0]} rows from {snap}")
        return px
    print("[SYNTHETIC] no network and no snapshot: generating a random walk. Numbers below are NOT real.")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    idx = pd.bdate_range(start, end or pd.Timestamp.today().normalize())
    px = pd.DataFrame({t: 100 * np.exp(np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.0004, 0.02 if "USD" in t else 0.011, len(idx))))
                       for t in tickers}, index=idx)
    return px
# --- course helper: one LLM wrapper, guarded. If no key -> deterministic MOCK so the notebook runs end-to-end. ---
import os, json, re

API_KEY = None
try:
    from google.colab import userdata
    API_KEY = userdata.get("GEMINI_API_KEY")
except Exception:
    API_KEY = os.environ.get("GEMINI_API_KEY")

MOCK_MODE = not bool(API_KEY)
if MOCK_MODE:
    print("No GEMINI_API_KEY found -> llm() runs in MOCK mode (fixed, deterministic answers; labelled as such).")

def _mock(prompt, json_schema):
    """Fixed answers so every cell below runs offline. The mock summary deliberately contains one wrong number
    (80% instead of 79.5%) so that the source-check cell has something to catch."""
    p = prompt.lower()
    if json_schema is not None and "mica" in p:
        return {"classifications": [
            {"asset": "USDC", "mica_category": "EMT", "reason": "references one fiat currency 1:1; issuer must be a credit institution or EMI"},
            {"asset": "stETH", "mica_category": "other crypto-asset", "reason": "not a stablecoin; represents staked ETH plus rewards; issued by a protocol"},
            {"asset": "UNI", "mica_category": "other crypto-asset", "reason": "governance token, no claim on assets, no reference to fiat"}]}
    if "governance" in p or "proposal" in p:
        return ("[MOCK] The proposal raises the wstETH loan-to-value on Aave v3 Ethereum from 78.5% to 80% and the "
                "liquidation threshold from 81% to 82%, keeps the liquidation bonus at 6%, and raises the supply cap "
                "to 1.2M wstETH. Risk provider Chaos Labs supports it; the vote closes on 20 November 2026.")
    return "[MOCK] no canned answer for this prompt."

def llm(prompt, system=None, json_schema=None, temperature=0):
    """Single entry point for LLM calls. Returns text, or a dict when json_schema is given.
    Ports to any provider: only this function changes."""
    if MOCK_MODE:
        return _mock(prompt, json_schema)
    from google import genai
    from google.genai import types
    client = genai.Client(api_key=API_KEY)
    cfg = dict(temperature=temperature, system_instruction=system)
    if json_schema is not None:
        cfg.update(response_mime_type="application/json", response_schema=json_schema)
    r = client.models.generate_content(model="gemini-2.5-flash", contents=prompt,
                                       config=types.GenerateContentConfig(**cfg))
    return json.loads(r.text) if json_schema is not None else r.text.strip()

print("llm() ready —", "MOCK" if MOCK_MODE else "live Gemini")

title: Week 8 — Digital assets, on-chain data and DeFi
section: Block B — Lab 1: a constant-product pool from one equation
text:
Block B — Lab 1: a constant-product pool from one equation
A pool holds two reserves, x (say ETH) and y (say USDC). The rule is that a swap must leave the product x · y = k unchanged (before fees). Everything else — price, slippage, LP returns — follows from that one line.
Spot price of x in units of y: p = y / x. A trader who puts in dx gets out dy = y − k / (x + dx). The fee (0.3% on Uniswap v2-style pools) is taken on the way in and stays in the pool, which is how LPs earn.

class Pool:
    """Constant-product AMM (x*y = k) with a fee on input, Uniswap-v2 style."""
    def __init__(self, x, y, fee=0.003):
        self.x, self.y, self.fee = float(x), float(y), fee
    @property
    def price(self):            # y per 1 x  (e.g. USDC per ETH)
        return self.y / self.x
    @property
    def k(self):
        return self.x * self.y
    def quote_x_for_y(self, dx):
        """How much y you get for dx of x, without changing the pool."""
        dx_net = dx * (1 - self.fee)
        return self.y - self.k / (self.x + dx_net)
    def swap_x_for_y(self, dx):
        dy = self.quote_x_for_y(dx)
        self.x += dx; self.y -= dy          # the full dx enters the pool: k grows by the fee
        return dy

pool = Pool(x=1_000, y=3_000_000)           # 1,000 ETH and 3,000,000 USDC -> spot 3,000 USDC/ETH
print("spot price:", pool.price, "| k:", f"{pool.k:.3e}")

🔍 CHECK (bet 1). You sell 100 ETH (10% of the pool’s ETH reserve). Before running: what price per ETH do you actually receive versus the spot 3,000, and where is the pool price after the trade? Write both numbers down.

dx = 100
dy = pool.quote_x_for_y(dx)
exec_price = dy / dx
p_after = (pool.y - dy) / (pool.x + dx)
print(f"received {dy:,.0f} USDC for {dx} ETH -> execution price {exec_price:,.1f}  ({exec_price/pool.price-1:+.2%} vs spot)")
print(f"pool price after the trade: {p_after:,.1f}  ({p_after/pool.price-1:+.2%} vs spot)")

Two different numbers, both called “price impact” in conversation. Execution price ≈ p·x/(x+dx) → about −9% for a 10% trade; pool price after ≈ p·x²/(x+dx)² → about −17%. Neither is a fee: the pool simply has fewer USDC per ETH left. The curve is the market maker.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
sizes = np.array([0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50])
rows = []
for s in sizes:
    dx = s * pool.x; dy = pool.quote_x_for_y(dx)
    rows.append([s, dy/dx, dy/dx/pool.price - 1, (pool.y-dy)/(pool.x+dx)/pool.price - 1])
impact = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trade / reserve", "execution price", "exec vs spot", "pool price after vs spot"])
display(impact.round(4))
impact.set_index("trade / reserve")[["exec vs spot", "pool price after vs spot"]].plot(
    figsize=(8, 3.5), logx=True, marker="o", title="Price impact vs trade size (share of the x reserve)")
plt.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.5); plt.ylabel("vs spot"); plt.show()


🔍 CHECK — the assistant’s swap function
Asked to “write a function that swaps ETH for USDC in a constant-product pool with a 0.3% fee”, the assistant produced the cell below. It runs and prints numbers. It contains two errors. Compare its answers with the Pool class above for the same 100 ETH trade before opening the solution.

# --- as produced by the assistant (do not trust) ---
def swap_assistant(x, y, dx, fee=0.3):
    price = y / x
    dy = dx * price * (1 - fee)        # output at the current price, minus the fee
    return dy, (y - dy) / (x + dx)     # amount out, new pool price

for dx in [1, 100, 500]:
    dy, p_new = swap_assistant(1_000, 3_000_000, dx)
    print(f"sell {dx:>3} ETH -> {dy:,.0f} USDC | execution {dy/dx:,.1f} | pool price after {p_new:,.1f}")



Solution (open after you have tried)


dy = dx * price is a linear quote: it ignores the curve. Selling 500 ETH gets you 500 × 3,000 = 1.5M USDC minus fee, whatever the reserve — so the execution price never moves, slippage is zero, and the pool would go negative on a large enough trade. The correct output is y - k/(x + dx_net): the pool keeps x·y = k, so every unit you sell is priced a little lower than the last. The “pool price after” it prints only looks reasonable because it is computed from wrong dy.
fee=0.3 is 30%, not 0.3%. Percent vs decimal — the same silent error as the week-2 FRED yields. With a 30% fee the 1-ETH trade returns 2,100 USDC instead of ~2,991.

Rule: whenever a function returns money, test it on a trade of size 0 (must return 0) and on a trade the size of the whole reserve (must not drain the pool).


# Corrected version — same signature, curve respected, fee as a decimal
def swap(x, y, dx, fee=0.003):
    k = x * y
    dx_net = dx * (1 - fee)
    dy = y - k / (x + dx_net)
    return dy, (y - dy) / (x + dx)

for dx in [0, 1, 100, 500, 100_000]:
    dy, p_new = swap(1_000, 3_000_000, dx)
    print(f"sell {dx:>7,} ETH -> {dy:>12,.0f} USDC | pool price after {p_new:,.1f} | pool never below 0 USDC: {3_000_000 - dy > 0}")



LP value vs holding
An LP deposits both assets and owns a share of the pool. When the price moves, arbitrageurs trade against the pool until its price matches the market — and that rebalancing sells the LP’s winner and buys the loser. So the LP’s position is worth less than simply holding the two coins, by an amount that depends only on the price ratio r = p_now / p_deposit:
\[\frac{\text{LP value}}{\text{hold value}} = \frac{2\sqrt{r}}{1 + r}\]
That gap is called impermanent loss (a bad name: it is a real loss unless the price returns). Fees are what the LP is paid to bear it.
🔍 CHECK (bet 2). ETH doubles (r = 2). Before running: by what percentage is the LP position worth less than just holding? Write the number.

def lp_vs_hold(r):
    """Value of a constant-product LP position divided by the value of holding the deposited coins, for price ratio r."""
    return 2 * np.sqrt(r) / (1 + r)

# Same thing computed the long way, from the pool, so the formula is not taken on faith
x0, y0 = 1_000, 3_000_000; p0 = y0 / x0; k = x0 * y0
r = 2.0; p1 = p0 * r
x1, y1 = np.sqrt(k / p1), np.sqrt(k * p1)          # reserves after arbitrage brings the pool price to p1
lp_value = y1 + x1 * p1                            # in USDC
hold_value = y0 + x0 * p1
print(f"price 2x: LP value {lp_value:,.0f} | hold value {hold_value:,.0f} | LP/hold {lp_value/hold_value:.4f} | formula {lp_vs_hold(r):.4f}")
print(f"impermanent loss at 2x: {lp_vs_hold(r)-1:+.2%}")



🔍 CHECK — the assistant’s impermanent-loss curve
Asked to “plot impermanent loss as a function of the price ratio”, the assistant wrote the cell below. It plots a smooth curve. Compare the value at r = 2 with the number you just computed.

# --- as produced by the assistant (do not trust) ---
ratios = np.linspace(0.2, 5, 200)
x0, y0 = 1_000, 3_000_000; k = x0 * y0; p0 = y0 / x0
initial_value = y0 + x0 * p0
il_assistant = []
for r in ratios:
    p = p0 * r
    lp_value = np.sqrt(k / p) * p + np.sqrt(k * p)     # value of the rebalanced reserves at the new price
    il_assistant.append(lp_value / initial_value - 1)
il_assistant = pd.Series(il_assistant, index=ratios)
print("assistant's 'impermanent loss' at r=2:", f"{il_assistant.loc[2.0] if 2.0 in il_assistant.index else np.interp(2.0, ratios, il_assistant.values):+.2%}")
il_assistant.plot(figsize=(8, 3.5), title="Impermanent loss vs price ratio (assistant version)"); plt.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.5); plt.show()



Solution (open after you have tried)

The benchmark is wrong. The assistant divides by the initial value of the deposit, so at r = 2 it reports +41% — the LP made money, and the chart shows a “loss” that is positive whenever price goes up. Impermanent loss is defined against holding the same coins: at r = 2 holding is worth 1.5× the initial value, the LP position 1.414×, and the loss is 1.414/1.5 − 1 = −5.7%. Same LP value, different denominator, opposite conclusion.
This is the general form of the bug: a return is always relative to something; the assistant picks the denominator that is easiest to code. Ask “compared to what?” for every percentage a model or a person gives you.


# Corrected: benchmark = holding the deposited coins at the new price
il = pd.Series([lp_vs_hold(r) - 1 for r in ratios], index=ratios)
table = pd.DataFrame({"price ratio r": [0.25, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.25, 2, 3, 4, 5]})
table["LP / hold"] = lp_vs_hold(table["price ratio r"]).round(4)
table["impermanent loss"] = (table["LP / hold"] - 1).map("{:+.2%}".format)
display(table)
il.plot(figsize=(8, 3.5), title="Impermanent loss vs price ratio (vs holding)"); plt.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.5); plt.ylabel("LP/hold − 1"); plt.show()



Fee income vs impermanent loss
Fees are the other side of the ledger. If the pool turns over a fraction v of its reserves every day at fee f, the LP earns roughly f · v · 365 per year on the pool’s value. Whether providing liquidity beats holding is then a race between that yield and the impermanent loss the price path produces.
🔍 CHECK (bet 3, sign only). Daily volume equal to 20% of pool value, 0.3% fee, held for one year, and ETH ends the year at 2×. Before running: does the LP finish ahead of or behind holding? Write + or −.

fee, days = 0.003, 365
vol_over_tvl = np.array([0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50, 1.00])     # daily volume as a share of pool value
fee_yield = fee * vol_over_tvl * days                              # annual fee income as share of pool value
fees = pd.DataFrame({"daily volume / TVL": vol_over_tvl, "annual fee yield": fee_yield})
for r in [1.25, 2, 3]:
    fees[f"net vs hold @ {r}x"] = fee_yield + (lp_vs_hold(r) - 1)
display(fees.set_index("daily volume / TVL").apply(lambda col: col.map("{:+.1%}".format)))
print("break-even daily volume/TVL to cover IL at 2x:", f"{-(lp_vs_hold(2)-1) / (fee * days):.3f}")



LP on a real price path
The curve above assumes a single jump. On a real path the LP position is marked every day: Pool reserves follow the price, fees accrue with assumed volume. We use ETH-USD from the course loader (live → snapshot → synthetic). If the loader printed [SYNTHETIC], the path below is a random walk and the numbers are only a pipeline test.

px = load_prices(["ETH-USD"], start="2022-01-01").ffill().dropna()
eth = px["ETH-USD"]
p0 = eth.iloc[0]
x0 = 1.0; y0 = x0 * p0                     # deposit 1 ETH and the same value in USDC
k = x0 * y0
r_path = eth / p0
lp = pd.DataFrame(index=eth.index)
lp["hold"] = y0 + x0 * eth                             # value in USDC of holding the deposit
lp["lp_no_fees"] = 2 * np.sqrt(k * eth)                # value of the rebalanced reserves at each price
lp["il"] = lp["lp_no_fees"] / lp["hold"] - 1
vol_over_tvl = 0.20                                    # assumption — replace with pool data in the homework
lp["fees_cum"] = (fee * vol_over_tvl * lp["lp_no_fees"]).cumsum()
lp["lp_with_fees"] = lp["lp_no_fees"] + lp["fees_cum"]
print(f"deposit {p0:,.0f} USDC/ETH -> today {eth.iloc[-1]:,.0f} (r = {r_path.iloc[-1]:.2f})")
print(f"hold {lp['hold'].iloc[-1]:,.0f} | LP no fees {lp['lp_no_fees'].iloc[-1]:,.0f} (IL {lp['il'].iloc[-1]:+.1%}) | LP with fees {lp['lp_with_fees'].iloc[-1]:,.0f}")
lp[["hold", "lp_no_fees", "lp_with_fees"]].plot(figsize=(10, 4), title="1 ETH + USDC: hold vs LP (constant product), fees at assumed 20%/day volume/TVL"); plt.ylabel("USDC"); plt.show()

🔍 CHECK. The fee line depends entirely on the vol_over_tvl assumption. Change it to 0.05 and to 0.50 and see when the LP crosses hold. The honest version of this chart needs the pool’s actual volume, which is what the DefiLlama block gives you next.

title: Week 8 — Digital assets, on-chain data and DeFi
section: Block C — Lab 2: protocol data through public APIs
text:
Block C — Lab 2: protocol data through public APIs
DefiLlama aggregates on-chain data per protocol: TVL (value locked), fees (what users pay) and revenue (the part the protocol or its token keeps; the rest goes to LPs, stakers or validators). CoinGecko gives token price and market cap. Both are free and need no key. Both go through the same three-tier loader: live → dated snapshot in data/ → a small SYNTHETIC table labelled as such.

import requests, glob, datetime as dt

SLUGS = {"uniswap": "uniswap", "aave": "aave", "lido": "lido-dao"}      # DefiLlama slug -> CoinGecko id
def _get(url, timeout=15):
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, headers={"User-Agent": "ese-course"}); r.raise_for_status(); return r.json()

def load_protocol_metrics(slugs=SLUGS, cache_dir="data"):
    os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
    stamp = dt.date.today().isoformat()
    snap = f"{cache_dir}/protocol_metrics_{stamp}.csv"
    try:
        rows = []
        for slug, cg in slugs.items():
            tvl = _get(f"https://api.llama.fi/tvl/{slug}")
            fees = _get(f"https://api.llama.fi/summary/fees/{slug}?dataType=dailyFees")
            rev = _get(f"https://api.llama.fi/summary/fees/{slug}?dataType=dailyRevenue")
            rows.append(dict(protocol=slug, tvl=float(tvl), fees_30d=fees.get("total30d"), revenue_30d=rev.get("total30d")))
        m = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("protocol")
        cg = _get("https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/simple/price?ids=" + ",".join(slugs.values()) + "&vs_currencies=usd&include_market_cap=true")
        m["price"] = [cg[c]["usd"] for c in slugs.values()]
        m["market_cap"] = [cg[c]["usd_market_cap"] for c in slugs.values()]
        m["source"] = "live " + stamp
        m.to_csv(snap); print("[live] DefiLlama + CoinGecko; snapshot saved to", snap); return m
    except Exception as e:
        print("[warn] live fetch failed:", type(e).__name__)
    snaps = sorted(glob.glob(f"{cache_dir}/protocol_metrics_*.csv"))
    if snaps:
        m = pd.read_csv(snaps[-1], index_col=0); print("[snapshot]", snaps[-1]); return m
    print("[SYNTHETIC] illustrative order-of-magnitude numbers, NOT real data — do not quote them.")
    m = pd.DataFrame({
        "tvl":         [4.5e9, 25e9, 28e9],
        "fees_30d":    [80e6, 55e6, 90e6],
        "revenue_30d": [6e6, 9e6, 9e6],
        "price":       [8.0, 230.0, 1.10],
        "market_cap":  [5.0e9, 3.5e9, 1.0e9],
    }, index=pd.Index(list(slugs), name="protocol"))
    m["source"] = "SYNTHETIC"
    return m

metrics = load_protocol_metrics()
metrics

🔍 CHECK (bet 4). Three protocols, three business models: an exchange (Uniswap), a lender (Aave), a staking service (Lido). Before running: which has the highest annualised fees / TVL, and which the highest revenue / market cap? Write the two names.

m = metrics.copy()
m["fees_annual"] = m["fees_30d"] * 12
m["revenue_annual"] = m["revenue_30d"] * 12
m["fees / TVL"] = m["fees_annual"] / m["tvl"]
m["revenue / TVL"] = m["revenue_annual"] / m["tvl"]
m["revenue / mcap"] = m["revenue_annual"] / m["market_cap"]
m["take rate (rev/fees)"] = m["revenue_annual"] / m["fees_annual"]
out = m[["tvl", "fees_annual", "revenue_annual", "market_cap", "fees / TVL", "revenue / TVL", "revenue / mcap", "take rate (rev/fees)"]]
display(out.style.format({"tvl": "{:,.0f}", "fees_annual": "{:,.0f}", "revenue_annual": "{:,.0f}", "market_cap": "{:,.0f}",
                          "fees / TVL": "{:.1%}", "revenue / TVL": "{:.2%}", "revenue / mcap": "{:.1%}", "take rate (rev/fees)": "{:.0%}"}))
print("source:", metrics["source"].iloc[0])

Read the ratios as a PM would read a SaaS dashboard: fees/TVL is asset turnover (how hard the capital works), take rate is what the protocol keeps of what users pay, revenue/mcap is the inverse of a price-to-sales multiple. An exchange turns its capital over daily; a lender or a staking service earns a spread on capital that sits. The ratios differ by an order of magnitude because the businesses differ, not because one is “better”.

TVL concentration
How concentrated is DeFi? The whole protocol list from DefiLlama, or a labelled synthetic list.

def load_tvl_table(cache_dir="data"):
    os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
    stamp = dt.date.today().isoformat(); snap = f"{cache_dir}/defillama_protocols_{stamp}.csv"
    try:
        js = _get("https://api.llama.fi/protocols")
        t = pd.DataFrame([{"name": p["name"], "category": p.get("category"), "tvl": p.get("tvl") or 0} for p in js])
        t = t[t["tvl"] > 0].sort_values("tvl", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
        t.to_csv(snap, index=False); print("[live] DefiLlama /protocols:", len(t), "protocols; snapshot", snap); return t, "live"
    except Exception as e:
        print("[warn] DefiLlama /protocols failed:", type(e).__name__)
    snaps = sorted(glob.glob(f"{cache_dir}/defillama_protocols_*.csv"))
    if snaps:
        print("[snapshot]", snaps[-1]); return pd.read_csv(snaps[-1]), "snapshot"
    print("[SYNTHETIC] illustrative list, NOT real data.")
    t = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Lido", "Aave", "EigenLayer", "ether.fi", "Sky", "Binance staked ETH", "Ethena", "Uniswap", "Morpho",
                               "Pendle", "Spark", "Rocket Pool", "Compound", "Curve", "Jito"] + [f"protocol_{i}" for i in range(16, 216)],
                      "tvl": [28e9, 25e9, 12e9, 8e9, 6e9, 6e9, 5e9, 4.5e9, 4e9, 4e9, 3e9, 3e9, 2.5e9, 2e9, 2e9]
                             + list(np.round(1.5e9 * 0.97 ** np.arange(200), 0))})
    t["category"] = "n/a"
    return t.sort_values("tvl", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True), "SYNTHETIC"

tvl_table, tvl_source = load_tvl_table()
total = tvl_table["tvl"].sum()
share = tvl_table["tvl"] / total
hhi = (share ** 2).sum()
print(f"[{tvl_source}] {len(tvl_table)} protocols | total TVL {total/1e9:,.1f}B | top-5 share {share.head(5).sum():.1%} | top-10 share {share.head(10).sum():.1%} | HHI {hhi:.3f}")
tvl_table.head(10).assign(share=share.head(10).map("{:.1%}".format))

🔍 CHECK (bet 5). You wrote a top-10 share before running. Now the interpretive question: DefiLlama counts the same ETH once in Lido (staked) and again in Aave if the stETH is deposited as collateral. Is the concentration you see over- or under-stated by that double counting? (Look for a category column: liquid staking and restaking are the layers most exposed to it.)


Reading a governance proposal with the LLM, then checking it against the source
Protocol parameters (collateral ratios, caps, fees) are changed by governance votes. The texts are long and full of numbers. An LLM summary is useful only with a mechanical check that every number in the summary exists in the source. llm() is mocked if no key; the mock deliberately contains one wrong number so the check has something to catch.

proposal = """
AIP-412 — Risk parameter update for wstETH on Aave v3 Ethereum (Chaos Labs)

Summary. We propose to increase the loan-to-value (LTV) of wstETH from 78.5% to 79.5% and the liquidation threshold
from 81% to 82%, reflecting deeper wstETH/ETH liquidity on-chain and lower realised volatility of the stETH/ETH rate
over the last 180 days. The liquidation bonus remains at 6%. We also propose raising the wstETH supply cap from 1.0M
to 1.2M wstETH, given current utilisation of 91% of the cap.

Risk analysis. The stETH/ETH secondary-market discount has stayed within 0.3% for 180 days. Under a 10% ETH price
shock with a simultaneous 2% stETH discount, simulated bad debt is below 50k USD. The oracle remains the Chainlink
wstETH/ETH × ETH/USD feed. Recommended: ARFC forum discussion closes 13 November 2026; on-chain vote closes
20 November 2026.
"""
summary = llm("Summarise this governance proposal in three sentences, keeping every parameter change with its old and new value.\n\n" + proposal,
              system="You are a DeFi risk analyst. Be precise; never invent numbers.")
print(summary)


def numbers_in(text):
    """All numeric tokens (with %, k, M) in a text, normalised as strings."""
    return set(re.findall(r"\d+(?:[.,]\d+)?", text))

src, summ = numbers_in(proposal), numbers_in(summary)
unsupported = sorted(summ - src)
print("numbers in summary:", sorted(summ))
print("NOT in source (possible hallucination):", unsupported if unsupported else "none")
missing = {"79.5", "82", "6", "1.2"} - summ
print("parameter values missing from the summary:", sorted(missing) if missing else "none")

🔍 CHECK. The check catches a number that is in the summary but not in the source. What does it not catch? (Two kinds of error survive it: a source number attached to the wrong parameter, and a correct number with the wrong direction — “from 80% to 78.5%”.) A number check is necessary, not sufficient — the same lesson as the RAG evals in week 4.

Five lenses, one protocol. The table below is a template: fill it for one protocol from the metrics table above (or your capstone protocol). Each cell must be a sentence with a fact you can point to (a contract audit date, an oracle name, a governance quorum, a peg history), not an adjective.

canvas = pd.DataFrame({

    "question":  ["Can the code lose the money? (audits, upgradeability, admin keys, bug history)",
                  "Where does the protocol get prices from, and what happens if that source is wrong for 10 minutes?",
                  "Who can change the parameters, how fast, and what is the quorum?",
                  "What backs the assets in the pool, and what breaks if the backing trades at a discount?",
                  "If 20% of TVL leaves today, does the protocol keep working?"],
    "what I found": ["", "", "", "", ""],
    "severity 1-5": [None] * 5,
    "evidence (link / number)": ["", "", "", "", ""],
})
canvas.set_index("lens")

Historical cases, one line each, are on the card; the exercise is to place each case in a row of this table. Every big DeFi loss fits one row — and most fit two, because an oracle failure is usually exploited through a lending contract, and a depeg becomes a liquidity crisis.
